clinical: Dry eye
An unstable tear film leaves the surface cells dry and speckled with tiny erosions, which causes stinging and blurred vision.
Corneal abrasion
Basal cells divide and slide across the wound to refill the gap, so a small scratch on the surface usually heals within a few days.

Limbus.description: The limbus is the narrow ring where the clear cornea meets the white sclera. Here the epithelium thickens, and the limbal stem cells, tucked between ridges of tissue called palisades of Vogt, keep renewing the corneal surface. Nearby, the conjunctiva's goblet cells make mucin for the tear film, and blood vessels run around the rim.
clinical: Limbal stem cell deficiency
If these stem cells are lost, for example after a chemical burn, the surface is taken over by conjunctiva-like tissue with blood vessels, which clouds the cornea.
Pterygium
A wedge of conjunctiva grows over the limbus onto the cornea, most often in people with long-term sun exposure.

Anterior cornea.description: Directly under the surface cells lies the epithelial basement membrane, which anchors them firmly in place. Below it, Bowman layer is a thin, cell-free sheet of collagen that does not regenerate, so injuries that reach it heal with a scar.
clinical: Recurrent corneal erosion
When the basement membrane is loose, as in basement membrane dystrophy, the surface cells peel away, often on waking, causing sharp pain.
Laser eye surgery (PRK)
PRK removes the surface cells and then reshapes the cornea by lasering Bowman layer and some of the stroma beneath it.
Corneal scarring
After injury, keratocytes turn into repair cells that lay down disordered collagen, so the scar is cloudy rather than clear.
Macular corneal dystrophy
An inherited fault in keratan sulphate processing causes abnormal deposits that cloud the stroma.

Posterior cornea.description: The back surface of the cornea faces the inside of the eye. It is lined by Descemet membrane, a basement membrane made by the endothelium, and a single layer of endothelial cells sits on the inner side of that membrane. The endothelium pumps fluid out of the stroma to keep it dehydrated and clear, so when these cells are lost the cornea swells and clouds. A thin collagen layer named after Dua lies between the stroma and Descemet membrane, though some experts doubt it is a separate layer.
clinical: Fuchs endothelial dystrophy
The endothelium slowly declines and Descemet membrane thickens with wart-like bumps called guttae, which typically cause blurred vision on waking.
Bullous keratopathy
When the endothelium can no longer pump fluid out, the stroma swells and painful blisters form on the surface of the cornea.

Drainage angle.description: The drainage angle is the narrow corner where the iris meets the cornea and sclera, and it is the main exit route for aqueous humour, the fluid that nourishes the front of the eye. Fluid filters through the trabecular meshwork, a porous sieve of tissue whose front edge is marked by Schwalbe line, and then enters Schlemm canal, a ring-shaped channel. From there it drains through collector channels into small veins that run through and just outside the sclera.
clinical: Primary open-angle glaucoma
Resistance to outflow through the trabecular meshwork raises eye pressure, which slowly damages the optic nerve.
Angle-closure glaucoma
If the iris blocks the drainage angle, fluid cannot leave the eye, and pressure can rise suddenly, causing severe pain and redness.
Neurotrophic keratopathy
Damage to the trigeminal nerve (its ophthalmic branch) leaves the cornea numb, so the surface epithelium heals poorly and can break down.
Laser eye surgery (LASIK)
The corneal flap cut severs corneal nerves, so sensation and tear production fall for months until the nerves regrow.

parts.description: Basal columnar cells form the single row of tall cells at the base of the corneal epithelium, resting on the basement membrane and anchored to it by hemidesmosomes (small attachment plaques). They are the only dividing cells of the central epithelium, and their daughter cells are pushed forward to become the wing and superficial layers. In a section, look for one neat row of tall cells with oval nuclei; weak attachment at this level underlies recurrent corneal erosion.

Limbal epithelial stem cells are the slowly dividing, unspecialised cells in the basal layer of the palisades of Vogt, which are radial ridges of epithelium in the limbus, the narrow rim where the cornea meets the sclera. Their daughter cells move inwards across the surface to renew the corneal epithelium. In a section they are small, dark basal cells with a large nucleus for their small amount of cytoplasm; if they are lost, conjunctival cells can spread over the cornea.

Wing cells are the middle layers of the corneal epithelium, usually two or three cells thick, lying between the basal cells below and the superficial cells above. Each cell is polygonal, with wing-like side processes that interlock with its neighbours and are held together by desmosomes (spot-like cell junctions). In a section they look like several layers of angular cells with round nuclei, and many of the fine corneal nerve endings run up between them.

Limbal epithelium is the thick, stratified squamous epithelium that overlies the limbus, the narrow rim where the cornea meets the sclera. It has more cell layers than the central corneal epithelium and contains the limbal stem cells in its basal layer. In a section it is noticeably thicker at the rim than in the centre, and its basal cells rest on the fibrous limbal stroma.

Superficial squamous cells form the outermost layer of the corneal epithelium, two or three cells thick, and face the tear film. They are flat, non-keratinised cells, meaning they keep their nuclei rather than hardening into a horny layer. Tight junctions seal them together, and their free surface carries tiny folds and a sugary coat, the glycocalyx, that holds the tear film. In a section they form the flat top layer with small, flattened nuclei; they are shed into the tears as the epithelium renews every 7-10 days.

Conjunctival goblet cells are mucin-secreting cells scattered among the stratified squamous epithelium of the conjunctiva, the thin mucous membrane that lines the eyelids and the front of the eye. They release mucin (MUC5AC) that spreads over the cornea and helps stabilise the tear film. Most are concentrated in the lower fornix and the nasal conjunctiva. In a section, look for pale, goblet-shaped cells with a basal nucleus and a cytoplasm full of mucin granules, which stain magenta in the periodic acid-Schiff (PAS) reaction.

The tear film is the thin fluid layer that coats the front of the eye. It has three layers: an outer oily (lipid) layer from the meibomian glands in the eyelids, a watery middle layer from the lacrimal (tear) glands, and an inner mucin layer from goblet cells and the glycocalyx, a sugary coat on the surface cells. It provides the main refracting (light-bending) surface of the eye at the air-tear interface, and is renewed with every blink. Dry-eye disease occurs when this film becomes unstable or too thin.

Bowman layer is a thin, acellular sheet of randomly arranged collagen fibrils lying between the epithelial basement membrane and the stroma. Because it is acellular, it does not regenerate, so an injury that reaches it heals with a scar rather than a clear surface. In a section, look for a homogeneous, cell-free band directly beneath the basement membrane, with no keratocytes or epithelial cells within it.

The epithelial basement membrane is a thin, specialised sheet of extracellular matrix made by the basal cells, lying between them and Bowman layer. It is built mainly of type IV collagen and laminin; hemidesmosomes (small attachment plaques) attach the basal cells to it, and anchoring fibrils (type VII collagen) fix it to the layer beneath. In an electron micrograph it appears as a thin, dense line between the basal cells and Bowman layer.

Stromal lamellae are the stacked, flat sheets of collagen that make up about 90% of the corneal thickness, lying between Bowman layer and Descemet membrane. Each lamella is a sheet of parallel type I collagen fibrils of uniform diameter, held at a regular spacing by proteoglycans carrying keratan sulphate; this regular packing is what makes the cornea transparent. Lamellae are best seen in electron micrographs, where they look like parallel fibril sheets; routine stains show the stroma as homogeneous. Corneal swelling disturbs the spacing and clouds the cornea.

Keratocytes are the flattened, branching fibroblast-like cells of the corneal stroma, lying in small spaces (lacunae) between the lamellae. They are linked to one another by gap junctions, maintain the collagen and ground substance of the stroma, and contain crystallin proteins (such as aldehyde dehydrogenase and transketolase) that keep the tissue transparent. After injury they can turn into repair fibroblasts and myofibroblasts, which can lead to haze and scarring. In a section they appear as small, flattened nuclei squeezed between the lamellae.

Pre-Descemet (Dua) layer is a thin, cell-free band of fine collagen fibrils lying between the back of the corneal stroma and Descemet membrane. It was described in 2013 by Harminder Dua and colleagues, which is why it bears his name, and some researchers still question whether it is a truly separate layer. It is easily missed in routine sections because it is so thin and contains no cells, and it matters mainly to surgeons who operate on the back of the cornea.

Descemet membrane is the thick basement membrane that the corneal endothelium makes, lying between the endothelium and the stroma (or Dua layer). It has an anterior non-banded part laid down before birth and a posterior banded part that the endothelium keeps producing throughout life, both built largely of type IV and type VIII collagen. In a section it appears as a smooth, homogeneous band behind the stroma, and it thickens with age.

Schwalbe line is the thin, grey-white ring at the outer edge of the cornea, marking the point where Descemet membrane ends. It forms the anterior border of the trabecular meshwork, the drainage tissue of the iris-cornea angle, and is seen when the angle is examined with a gonioscope (a special contact lens). It is a useful landmark for locating the meshwork.

The corneal endothelium is the single layer of flattened, hexagonal cells that lines the back of the cornea, facing the aqueous humour of the anterior chamber. Its cells pump fluid out of the stroma through ion pumps, keeping the stroma relatively dehydrated and therefore clear. Human endothelial cells do not divide much, so lost cells are not replaced well, and once the cell count falls too low the cornea swells and clouds. In a section, look for a thin layer of flat nuclei on the inner surface of Descemet membrane.

The limbal stroma is the fibrous connective tissue of the limbus, the transition zone between the clear cornea and the white sclera, and it carries blood vessels and nerves. Its stromal ridges project between the palisades of Vogt, which are radial ridges of epithelium that house the limbal stem cells. In a section, the palisades appear as epithelial ridges running towards the centre of the cornea, with limbal stroma between them.

The limbal vascular arcades are a ring of small blood vessels that encircles the cornea within the limbus, formed mainly by branches of the anterior ciliary arteries and conjunctival vessels. They nourish the limbus itself, while the cornea remains avascular, taking its oxygen from the air and its nutrients from tears and aqueous humour. In a section or on slit-lamp examination, look for this ring of vessels at the corneal edge; in disease, new vessels can grow inwards from it, causing corneal neovascularisation.

The sclera is the tough, white, opaque outer coat of the eyeball, made mainly of dense irregular connective tissue rich in type I collagen. It runs from the limbus at the front, where it joins the clear cornea, to the optic nerve at the back, and the episclera lies on its outer surface. In a section it appears as a dense, pink, irregularly woven band with relatively few blood vessels; the dense collagen is what makes it look white to the naked eye.

Schlemm canal is a ring-shaped, endothelium-lined channel in the sclera at the drainage angle, just outside the trabecular meshwork. It collects aqueous humour that has filtered through the meshwork and carries it into collector channels, which drain into the aqueous veins. In a section, look for a thin, flattened endothelium on a basement membrane, around a narrow, often collapsed lumen; raised outflow resistance in this channel and the meshwork is a major cause of high eye pressure in glaucoma.

Collector channels are small tubes that arise from the outer wall of Schlemm canal and carry aqueous humour away from the eye's drainage angle. They drain into aqueous veins, small veins that run through and just outside the sclera and join the episcleral venous system. In a section of the angle, look for thin-walled channels opening off the outer wall of the canal, and for these veins lying nearby in the sclera.

The trabecular meshwork is a sponge-like filter of collagen beams, each coated with trabecular cells, lying in the drainage angle between the iris and cornea. Aqueous humour passes through its spaces into Schlemm canal, and resistance to this flow in the meshwork helps set the normal eye pressure. On gonioscopy (examination of the angle with a special lens) it appears as a grey-brown, meshed band; increased resistance here is the main cause of primary open-angle glaucoma.

Stromal nerves are branches of the long ciliary nerves, which come from the ophthalmic division of the trigeminal nerve (V1). They enter the stroma radially at the limbus, lose their myelin sheaths as they reach the cornea so that it stays transparent, then turn forwards and pierce Bowman layer to supply the subbasal plexus. Their sensory input forms the afferent limb of the blink reflex, and loss of this supply causes neurotrophic keratopathy, a poorly healing corneal breakdown.
